anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst lies in the midline along the thyroid's descent path and moves with tongue protrusion; a branchial cyst is lateral (anterior to sternocleidomastoid).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Applied / Clinical.question: Monozygotic twins that are monochorionic and monoamniotic arise from splitting at:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Splitting at day 8–12 shares one chorion and one amnion; >day 13 gives conjoined twins, <day 3 gives dichorionic-diamniotic twins.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Fertilisation normally occurs in the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube — which is also the commonest site of ectopic implantation.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: A solid ball of about 16 blastomeres is called the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Cleavage produces the morula (~16 cells, day 3–4); fluid then accumulates to form the blastocyst.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Which part of the blastocyst gives rise to the embryo proper?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The inner cell mass (embryoblast) forms the embryo; the trophoblast forms the placenta and the blastocele is the cavity.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: hCG, the basis of the pregnancy test, is secreted by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The bilaminar disc consists of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The week-2 bilaminar disc is formed by the epiblast (dorsal) and hypoblast (ventral).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: All three definitive germ layers are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm — all from epiblast.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Gastrulation is best defined as the process that:
options: Converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Gastrulation (week 3) establishes the three germ layers and the body axes, converting a two-layered disc into a three-layered one.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The notochord arises from the primitive node and persists in the adult as the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The notochord induces neurulation and remains as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The first organ system to function in the embryo is the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The cardiovascular system is the first to function, with the heart beating around day 22.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Melanocytes, the adrenal medulla and the aorticopulmonary septum are all derivatives of:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: These are all neural crest derivatives — the neural crest is often called the 'fourth germ layer'.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The kidneys and gonads develop from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Intermediate mesoderm forms the urinary system and gonads; paraxial forms somites and lateral plate forms the cardiovascular system and serous membranes.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts is derived from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gut and airways, plus the liver, pancreas, thyroid, thymus and bladder.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close (~day 25) results in:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The cranial neuropore closes ~day 25 — failure produces anencephaly; failure of the caudal neuropore (~day 28) produces spina bifida.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The primitive streak establishes which feature of the embryo?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The primitive streak defines the craniocaudal axis, plus left–right and dorsal–ventral orientation.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The embryonic period (organogenesis), the time of greatest teratogen sensitivity, spans:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Weeks 3–8 constitute the embryonic period of organogenesis; from week 9 the fetal period (growth/function) begins.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Which membrane will become the future mouth?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The oropharyngeal membrane (bilaminar, lacking mesoderm) breaks down to form the mouth; the cloacal membrane forms the anal/urogenital openings.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: The umbilical cord normally contains:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta and one umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: Before it can implant, the blastocyst must first:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: The blastocyst must hatch from the zona pellucida (~day 5–6) before the trophoblast can implant into the endometrium.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.question: A persistent primitive streak may give rise to which tumour of the newborn?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Dev.explanation: Remnants of the primitive streak can form a sacrococcygeal teratoma, the commonest tumour of the newborn.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The heart develops from which type of mesoderm?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The heart arises from splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm (the cardiogenic area / primary heart field).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: Which is the correct cranial-to-caudal order of the primitive heart-tube dilatations?
options: Bulbus cordis → truncus arteriosus → atrium → ventricle → sinus venosus
Sinus venosus → atrium → ventricle → bulbus cordis → truncus arteriosus
Truncus arteriosus → bulbus cordis → ventricle → atrium → sinus venosus
Truncus arteriosus → ventricle → bulbus cordis → sinus venosus → atrium
Atrium → ventricle → bulbus cordis → truncus arteriosus → sinus venosus
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: From cranial to caudal: truncus arteriosus, bulbus cordis, primitive ventricle, primitive atrium, sinus venosus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: Normal cardiac looping proceeds to the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The heart tube normally loops to the right (D-loop); a left loop produces dextrocardia.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The truncus arteriosus is divided by the aorticopulmonary (spiral) septum into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The smooth-walled part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) is derived from the:
options: Left horn of the sinus venosus
Right horn of the sinus venosus
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The right horn of the sinus venosus is absorbed into the RA to form the smooth sinus venarum; the crista terminalis marks the junction.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes the:
options: Smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum)
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The left horn of the sinus venosus forms the coronary sinus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: At birth, closure of the foramen ovale is triggered mainly by:
options: A fall in left atrial pressure
A rise in left atrial pressure
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: Lung expansion increases pulmonary venous return, raising left atrial pressure, which presses septum primum against septum secundum to close the foramen ovale (→ fossa ovalis).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: An ostium primum ASD, associated with Down syndrome, results from failure of the septum primum to fuse with the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: An ostium primum defect (part of an AVSD) is failure of septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions; it is associated with Down syndrome.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The membranous interventricular septum is formed largely by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The membranous IV septum is formed by the endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges, closing the interventricular foramen last; failure causes a membranous VSD.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: Failure of the conotruncal septum to spiral results in:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: If the aorticopulmonary septum forms but does not spiral, the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary trunk from the LV — transposition of the great arteries.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: Defective migration of which cells underlies conotruncal anomalies (e.g. Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition)?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: Neural crest cells populate the conotruncal ridges that form the aorticopulmonary septum; their faulty migration causes conotruncal defects.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The 3rd pharyngeal arch arteries give rise to the:
options: Common carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The 3rd arch arteries form the common carotids and the proximal internal carotid arteries.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The ductus arteriosus is a derivative of which pharyngeal arch artery?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The ductus arteriosus develops from the left 6th arch artery; the 6th arches also form the pulmonary arteries.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The left arch of the aorta is derived from the ____ arch artery.
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The left 4th arch artery forms the arch of the aorta; the right 4th forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: Which fetal shunt allows blood to bypass the liver?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The ductus venosus shunts oxygenated umbilical-vein blood past the liver into the IVC.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus directs blood from the:
options: Right atrium to the left atrium
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta, bypassing the high-resistance fetal lungs.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The adult ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum; the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The medial umbilical ligaments are remnants of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The obliterated distal umbilical arteries form the medial umbilical ligaments; the urachus/allantois forms the (single) median umbilical ligament.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.question: The vessel carrying the most highly oxygenated blood in the fetus is the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular.explanation: The single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus; the two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The lower respiratory tract develops as an outgrowth of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: The respiratory diverticulum evaginates from the ventral wall of the foregut at ~week 4 via the laryngotracheal groove.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The cartilage and smooth muscle of the bronchial tree are derived from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Respiratory epithelium/glands are endoderm; the cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue and visceral pleura come from splanchnic mesoderm.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The trachea is separated from the oesophagus by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: The tracheo-oesophageal septum, formed by fusion of the TE ridges, divides the ventral trachea from the dorsal oesophagus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The commonest form of oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula is:
options: Proximal atresia with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: About 85% have proximal oesophageal atresia with a distal TOF, so the distal oesophagus communicates with the trachea.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: An inability to pass a nasogastric tube with antenatal polyhydramnios suggests:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Oesophageal atresia stops the fetus swallowing amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios) and the NG tube coils in the blind upper pouch; it is part of VACTERL.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Which is the correct order of the stages of lung development?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Embryonic → Pseudoglandular → Canalicular → Saccular → Alveolar ('Every Premature Child Should Ambulate').

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: In which stage do respiratory bronchioles first appear and viability becomes just possible?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: In the canalicular stage (~16–26 weeks) respiratory bronchioles and primitive alveoli form and type II pneumocytes begin surfactant, so survival is just possible at its end.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Most alveoli are formed:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: The alveolar stage runs from ~32 weeks to about 8 years, so most alveoli form after birth.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Surfactant is produced by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant (chiefly lecithin/dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine), which lowers alveolar surface tension.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: A lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio greater than 2 indicates:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: An L:S ratio > 2 reflects adequate surfactant and fetal lung maturity, usually reached by ~34–35 weeks.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is caused by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: RDS results from surfactant deficiency (usually prematurity), causing atelectasis, hypoxia and 'ground-glass' lungs with hyaline membranes.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: A term infant of a poorly-controlled diabetic mother is at increased risk of RDS because fetal hyperinsulinaemia:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production, so even a near-term infant of a diabetic mother may develop RDS.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Antenatal maternal corticosteroids are given before preterm delivery to:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate type II pneumocyte surfactant production, reducing the incidence and severity of RDS.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: Which structure forms the central tendon of the diaphragm?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: The septum transversum forms the central tendon; the other three sources form the crura, peripheral muscle and posterolateral portions.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) because the septum transversum:
options: Forms at cervical levels then descends
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: The septum transversum originates at cervical levels C3–5 and descends, carrying the phrenic nerve with it.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: A Bochdalek congenital diaphragmatic hernia is due to failure of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane (usually left posterolateral) to close allows abdominal viscera into the thorax.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: The main cause of death in congenital diaphragmatic hernia is:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Herniated viscera compress the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia (and pulmonary hypertension) — the chief cause of death.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.question: A mass of non-functioning lung tissue supplied by a systemic (aortic) artery and lacking a bronchial connection is a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory.explanation: Pulmonary sequestration is non-functioning lung with no bronchial connection and an anomalous systemic arterial supply from the aorta.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk and ends at the:
options: Major duodenal papilla (2nd part of duodenum)
Proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The foregut extends to the major duodenal papilla in the 2nd part of the duodenum, where the coeliac and SMA territories meet.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The midgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery and extends to the:
options: Proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The midgut runs from the distal duodenum to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal third of the transverse colon.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Pain from a midgut structure (e.g. early appendicitis) is classically referred to the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Midgut visceral pain is referred to the periumbilical region; foregut pain is epigastric and hindgut pain is suprapubic.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: During development the stomach rotates 90° clockwise, so that the:
options: Pylorus moves to the left and down
Right vagus supplies the anterior wall
Left vagus supplies the anterior wall
Lesser curvature becomes the dorsal border
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Clockwise rotation carries the left surface (and left vagus) anteriorly, so the left vagus supplies the anterior wall and the right vagus the posterior wall.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The greater curvature of the stomach develops from the ____ border of the primitive stomach.
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The dorsal border grows faster and becomes the greater curvature; the ventral border becomes the lesser curvature.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The spleen develops within the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The spleen (mesodermal) develops in the dorsal mesogastrium and is supplied by the splenic artery from the coeliac trunk.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The uncinate process and inferior part of the pancreatic head are formed by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates posteriorly to fuse with the dorsal bud, forming the uncinate process and inferior head.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: A ring of pancreatic tissue encircling and obstructing the duodenum is a(n):
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: An annular pancreas results from abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud so tissue encircles the duodenum, causing obstruction.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Physiological herniation of the midgut into the umbilical cord occurs around week:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The midgut herniates physiologically around week 6 because of rapid gut growth and the large liver, returning by about week 10.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The total rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery is:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The midgut rotates a total of 270° anticlockwise (90° while herniated plus 180° on return) around the SMA axis.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: A persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct produces a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Failure of the vitelline duct to regress leaves a Meckel's diverticulum, which may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Incomplete midgut rotation predisposes the newborn to:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Malrotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base and Ladd's bands, predisposing to midgut volvulus — a surgical emergency.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The urorectal septum partitions the cloaca into a ventral urogenital sinus and a dorsal anorectal canal.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: The pectinate line of the anal canal marks the junction between:
options: Mesoderm and endoderm of the bladder
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: The pectinate line represents the former cloacal membrane — the endoderm (hindgut)/ectoderm (proctodeum) junction — explaining the dual supply of the anal canal.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Bilious vomiting with a 'double-bubble' sign in a neonate with Down syndrome indicates:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Duodenal atresia (failed recanalisation) causes proximal obstruction with the double-bubble sign and is associated with trisomy 21.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Projectile NON-bilious vomiting at 4 weeks of age with a palpable 'olive' suggests:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes projectile non-bilious vomiting (the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla) with a palpable pyloric 'olive'.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: A newborn with abdominal contents herniating through the umbilicus within a peritoneal/amniotic sac has:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Omphalocele is failure of the midgut to return, herniating into the cord within a peritoneal/amniotic sac and is associated with chromosomal anomalies; gastroschisis has no sac.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.question: Absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon (failure of neural crest migration) defines:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is aganglionosis of the distal bowel from arrested neural crest migration, causing functional obstruction and failure to pass meconium.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The urinary and genital systems both develop from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: Both arise from intermediate mesoderm (the urogenital ridge) on the posterior body wall.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The definitive (permanent) kidney is the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The metanephros is the definitive kidney; the pronephros degenerates and the mesonephros is transient (its duct persists).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The ureteric bud (an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct) forms the entire collecting system; the nephron comes from the metanephric blastema.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The nephron (glomerulus to distal convoluted tubule) is formed by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The metanephric blastema forms the nephron proper; the ureteric bud forms the collecting system, and they meet at the collecting duct/DCT junction.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: A horseshoe kidney remains low in the abdomen because its ascent is blocked by the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The fused lower poles of a horseshoe kidney are caught beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: Bilateral renal agenesis leads to which sequence?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: Absent kidneys cause oligohydramnios and the Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures and Potter facies.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The bladder trigone is derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The trigone forms from the absorbed mesonephric ducts (mesoderm); the rest of the bladder epithelium is endoderm from the urogenital sinus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The urachus (allantois remnant) becomes the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The urachus runs from the bladder apex to the umbilicus and obliterates to form the median umbilical ligament; a remnant can form a urachal cyst/fistula.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The SRY gene product directs the indifferent gonad to become a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: SRY encodes testis-determining factor, causing the medullary cords to form a testis (Sertoli and Leydig cells).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: Anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells causes:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: AMH causes the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts to regress; testosterone separately maintains the Wolffian ducts.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: Which hormone maintains the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: Testosterone from Leydig cells maintains the Wolffian ducts (→ epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle); DHT acts on the external genitalia and prostate.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The prostate and external male genitalia depend chiefly on:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: DHT (from testosterone via 5α-reductase) drives development of the prostate, penis and scrotum.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: In the absence of SRY, AMH and testosterone, the genital ducts develop into:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The female pathway is the default: without testis hormones the Müllerian ducts persist and the Wolffian ducts regress.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: The uterus, uterine tubes and upper vagina are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina; the lower vagina comes from the sinovaginal bulbs.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: In the female, the gubernaculum gives rise to the:
options: Ovarian ligament and round ligament of the uterus
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: The female gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus (passing through the inguinal canal).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: Hypospadias results from failure of fusion of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: Incomplete fusion of the urethral folds leaves the urethral meatus on the ventral penis; the foreskin should be preserved for surgical repair.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: A 46,XY infant raised female with testes but no uterus, and a blind vagina, most likely has:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: In complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY, defective androgen receptor) the external phenotype is female, testes are present, and AMH still causes Müllerian regression so there is no uterus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.question: A bicornuate uterus results from:
options: Incomplete fusion of the paramesonephric ducts
Failure of the vaginal plate to canalise
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary.explanation: Incomplete caudal fusion of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts produces a bicornuate uterus (part of a spectrum with septate and didelphys uteri).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: How many pharyngeal arches form, and which one leaves no adult derivatives?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: Six arches form (1, 2, 3, 4, 6); the 5th arch regresses and forms no adult structures.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The muscles of mastication are derived from which pharyngeal arch?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 1st (mandibular) arch forms the muscles of mastication and is supplied by CN V₃; Meckel's cartilage forms the malleus and incus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The muscles of facial expression and the stapes are derived from the ____ arch, supplied by CN ____.
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 2nd (hyoid) arch forms the muscles of facial expression and the stapes and is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: Stylopharyngeus, the only muscle of the 3rd arch, is supplied by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is the sole 3rd-arch muscle and is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is derived from the 4th arch (superior laryngeal nerve) rather than the 6th?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: Cricothyroid is the 4th-arch muscle supplied by the (external) superior laryngeal nerve; all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are 6th arch (recurrent laryngeal).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The middle ear cavity and auditory tube are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 1st pharyngeal pouch (tubotympanic recess) forms the middle ear cavity, mastoid antrum and auditory tube.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The palatine tonsil develops from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 2nd pharyngeal pouch forms the epithelium and crypts of the palatine tonsil.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus are both derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 3rd pharyngeal pouch forms the inferior parathyroids (dorsal) and the thymus (ventral); the thymus's long descent drags the inferior parathyroids below the superior ones.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The ultimobranchial body of the 4th pouch (with neural crest cells) gives rise to the calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The external acoustic meatus is derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The 1st pharyngeal cleft (ectoderm) forms the external acoustic meatus; the 1st membrane forms the tympanic membrane and the 1st pouch the middle ear.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: A painless fluctuant swelling in the lateral neck anterior to sternocleidomastoid, from a persistent cervical sinus, is a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: A branchial cyst arises from remnants of the cervical sinus (2nd cleft) and lies in the lateral neck anterior to sternocleidomastoid; a thyroglossal cyst is midline.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The anterior two-thirds (1st arch) has general sensation via the lingual nerve (V₃) and taste via the chorda tympani (VII).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives both general and taste sensation from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The posterior third (3rd arch) is supplied for both general sensation and taste by CN IX (a small posterior area by CN X).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: All the muscles of the tongue are supplied by CN XII except:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus (CN X, pharyngeal plexus); all other tongue muscles (from occipital myotomes) are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: The thyroid gland first appears as a diverticulum at the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: The thyroid begins as a midline endodermal diverticulum at the foramen caecum and descends via the thyroglossal duct.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: A midline neck cyst that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue is a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst lies in the midline along the thyroid's descent path and elevates on tongue protrusion (its tract is attached to the tongue base).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: Cleft lip is failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence; cleft palate is failure of fusion of the palatine shelves.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.question: Thymic and parathyroid aplasia (immunodeficiency + hypocalcaemia) from failure of the 3rd and 4th pouches occurs in:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) results from failed development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, causing thymic and parathyroid aplasia with conotruncal cardiac defects.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The central nervous system develops from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The neural tube forms the CNS (brain and spinal cord); the neural crest forms most of the PNS.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: In the developing neural tube, sensory neurons are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The dorsal alar plate forms sensory neurons (dorsal horn); the ventral basal plate forms motor neurons (ventral horn).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The groove separating the alar and basal plates is the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The sulcus limitans separates the alar (sensory) from the basal (motor) plate in the cord and brainstem.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: Which CNS cell type is derived from mesoderm rather than neuroectoderm?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: Microglia arise from mesodermal blood monocytes/macrophages; astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma and neurons are neuroectodermal.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia develop from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The telencephalon forms the cerebral hemispheres, cortex and basal ganglia; its cavities are the lateral ventricles.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The thalamus, hypothalamus and posterior pituitary are derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The diencephalon forms the thalamus, hypothalamus, retina/optic nerve, pineal and posterior pituitary; its cavity is the third ventricle.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The pons and cerebellum are both derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum; the myelencephalon forms the medulla — both share the fourth ventricle.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The cerebral aqueduct is the cavity of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The mesencephalon (midbrain) cavity narrows into the cerebral aqueduct, connecting the third and fourth ventricles.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The anterior pituitary arises from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth of oral (surface) ectoderm; the posterior pituitary is a diencephalic neuroectodermal downgrowth.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: A calcified suprasellar tumour arising from a Rathke's pouch remnant is a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: A craniopharyngioma arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch and often calcifies, compressing the optic chiasm.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The retina and optic nerve are embryologically derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The optic vesicles grow out from the diencephalon, so the retina and optic nerve are CNS (neuroectoderm).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: In the adult, the conus medullaris (end of the spinal cord) normally lies at about:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: Because the vertebral column grows faster than the cord, the conus ascends from ~L3 at birth to about L1/L2 in the adult.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: A lumbar puncture is performed below L2 because:
options: The vertebral canal is widest there
CSF is only present above L2
The cauda equina is absent below L2
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The cord ends at ~L1/L2 in the adult, so a needle at L3/4 or L4/5 enters the cauda equina in CSF without damaging the cord.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: The adrenal medulla and melanocytes are both derived from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: The adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells) and melanocytes are neural-crest derivatives, along with the PNS ganglia and Schwann cells.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: Anencephaly results from failure of closure of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close (~day 25) causes anencephaly; caudal neuropore failure causes spina bifida.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: Which neural tube defect involves herniation of BOTH meninges and neural tissue?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: A myelomeningocele herniates meninges and neural tissue, causing a neurological deficit; a meningocele contains meninges only.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: A Chiari II malformation, with cerebellar/brainstem herniation and hydrocephalus, classically accompanies:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation classically accompanies a myelomeningocele and causes hydrocephalus.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.question: Failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres, linked to trisomy 13 and alcohol, is:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System.explanation: Holoprosencephaly is failure of forebrain cleavage, causing midline facial defects; it is associated with trisomy 13 and fetal alcohol exposure.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The somites are formed by segmentation of the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm segments craniocaudally into pairs of somites, whose derivatives are the sclerotome, myotome and dermatome.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The sclerotome of a somite gives rise to the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The sclerotome forms the axial skeleton (vertebrae and ribs); the myotome forms skeletal muscle and the dermatome forms dorsal dermis.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: A vertebra forms by resegmentation, in which:
options: The caudal half of one sclerotome fuses with the cranial half of the next
The myotome fuses with the sclerotome
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Resegmentation (caudal half of one sclerotome + cranial half of the next) makes the vertebra intersegmental, so spinal nerves exit between vertebrae.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc is derived from the:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The notochord persists only as the nucleus pulposus; the surrounding annulus fibrosus is sclerotome-derived.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The flat bones of the skull vault form by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The calvaria (and facial bones and clavicle) form by intramembranous ossification directly within mesenchyme; the skull base and long bones are endochondral.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The facial skeleton (viscerocranium) is derived mainly from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Neural crest cells migrating through the pharyngeal arches form the facial skeleton, largely by intramembranous ossification.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Achondroplasia, causing short limbs with a normal trunk, results from a mutation in:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: An activating FGFR3 mutation impairs endochondral ossification at the growth plate, producing short limbs with a relatively normal trunk but an enlarged head (frontal bossing).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The skeleton of the limb is derived from the ____, while the limb muscles come from the ____.
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Limb bones and connective tissue come from lateral plate mesoderm; myoblasts migrate into the limb bud from the somites.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) controls which limb axis, and via which signal?
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The AER secretes FGFs that drive proximodistal outgrowth of the limb (stylopod → zeugopod → autopod).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: The zone of polarising activity (ZPA) patterns the anteroposterior axis (thumb to little finger) using:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The ZPA secretes Sonic hedgehog (Shh) to set the anteroposterior axis; ectopic ZPA/Shh activity causes polydactyly.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Separation of the fingers and toes is achieved by:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Programmed cell death removes the interdigital webs; failure of this apoptosis results in syndactyly.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Failure of interdigital apoptosis results in:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Persistence of the interdigital webs (failed apoptosis) causes syndactyly; extra ZPA signalling causes polydactyly.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: During development the upper limb rotates ____ so that the elbow points ____.
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: The upper limb rotates laterally so the elbow points backward (extensors posterior); the lower limb rotates medially so the knee points forward.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Limbs with absent long bones so the hands attach near the trunk ('flipper limbs'), classically due to thalidomide, describe:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Phocomelia (absent long bones) is the classic thalidomide embryopathy, occurring when the drug is taken during the limb-bud window (weeks 4–6).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Cardiac and most smooth muscle are derived from:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Cardiac muscle and most smooth muscle come from splanchnic mesoderm; skeletal muscle comes from somites/pharyngeal arches (the iris sphincter & dilator pupillae are the neuroectodermal exception).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Risk factors for developmental dysplasia of the hip include all EXCEPT:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: DDH is commoner in females, breech presentation, first-borns and those with a family history; male sex is not a risk factor (it is protective relative to female).

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: Absent or hypoplastic clavicles allowing the shoulders to meet in the midline, with delayed skull ossification, is characteristic of:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: Cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2) is a defect of intramembranous ossification causing absent/hypoplastic clavicles and delayed closure of the skull sutures/fontanelles.

anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.question: A wedge-shaped vertebra formed from a single ossification centre, causing congenital scoliosis, is a:
anatomy__EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & L.explanation: A hemivertebra develops when one side of a vertebra fails to form, producing a wedge shape and congenital scoliosis.
